title: Ash and the Whispering Woods
markdown:
The moonbeams lay like soft white pillows over the sleepy hills. Ash, a little elf with eyes as still and deep as pond water, smoothed his simple clothes and felt a quiet flutter start in his chest. Tonight was a walking night. He wanted to ask the Old Pine Tree a gentle question that had been nuzzling at his mind for a long, long time.

Corvus sat on a low mossy branch nearby, feathers as dark and shiny as the deepest night. He ruffled them once and peered at a scrap of bark in his claw. Dots and swirls covered it. More cobweb than path.

“Are we ready, Ash?” he murmured, voice low and mellow. “My chart is ready. Though it does look a little… swirly.”

Ash smiled a slow soft smile. Corvus’s charts were always more feeling than drawing. “Yes, Corvus. The Old Pine Tree is waiting.”

They started into the quiet woods. Leaves rustled under small feet and quieter wings. The air smelled of pine needles and damp earth. Each tiny needle chimed like a far bell in the whispering wind. Ash loved this hush, when even the shadows seemed to be dreaming. Moonlight made silver coins of the puddles. A moth rested on Ash’s sleeve, then drifted off as if it too had somewhere gentle to be.

“Left here, Ash. Left!” Corvus pointed a sleek black wing toward a path that wound deeper into silvered shade. “The chart says a shiny rock that winks, then a turn past a very sleepy mushroom that dreams of dew.”

Ash turned left. The path was soft with needles. For a little while the woods agreed with the chart, or seemed to. Then the chiming swirled around them, and the path grew less certain. Corvus looked from bark to trees. His brow puzzled. He turned the scrap this way and that, as if a swirl might become a straight line if he only squinted harder.

“Hmm. That looks more like a patch of plump berries than a shiny rock. And that mushroom is wide awake. Perhaps the chart has taken a little nap.”

Ash tasted a berry. It was real, and sweet, and not a rock at all. The mushroom blinked dew from its cap and did not look the least bit sleepy. Corvus gave a small sorry caw and tucked the bark under one wing.

A warm buttery smell drifted toward them, as sweet as honey and as welcome as a hug. Around a bend that was no longer quite a path sat a small cozy house among the trees. A baker named Bartholomew stood there, white flour like soft snow on his round cheeks, polishing a row of gentle lanterns. Warm light pooled on the doorstep. A tray of rolls cooled on the sill. His smile was as warm as bread. His eyes twinkled like far-off stars.

Ash felt a little flutter about his question, and Corvus’s swirly chart did not help. “Excuse me, sir,” he whispered, polite as a small stream. “We are trying to find the Old Pine Tree. Do you know the clearest way?”

Bartholomew chuckled, a sound like pebbles rolling in water. He looked kindly at the smudged bark. “Ah. A muddled chart. The Old Pine Tree is much easier to find if you follow the stream. It flows right past its great wise roots. The stream is always clear. It never gets swirly the way charts do when they try to be too clever.”

He reached into a basket and offered Ash a warm buttery roll. “For the walk, young elf.”

Ash took it. Warmth spread through his fingers. “Thank you, Bartholomew. A clear stream sounds much better than a swirly chart.”

Corvus nodded his sleek head and let out a happy soft caw. “Yes. A stream. No more squinting at smudges.”

They followed the sound of water. It was a small sound at first, like someone humming in the next room. Ash broke the roll and shared a piece with Corvus. The stream grew louder, then brighter where moonlight found it. They kept to its bank. No swirls. No winking rocks that were berries. Only water knowing where to go.

Soon the murmur was a welcome, and there it was: the big Old Pine Tree, ancient branches reaching like gentle arms toward the moon. Its roots drank from the stream the way a friend takes a cup. Ash stood a moment with the last of the roll still warm in his pocket. He listened to the needles. He thought of the question that had been nuzzling him for so long. Then he whispered it, close to the bark, as if the tree might be a little sleepy too.

The tree answered in a rustle that settled in his chest like a smooth stone.

The walk back felt clear. They followed the stream the other way, and the chiming pinewood was familiar now. Bartholomew’s lanterns were still glowing when they passed the little house. The baker lifted a floury hand and did not ask if they had found the tree. He could see that they had.

As the first rosy light painted the eastern sky, they reached their cozy home. Ash set the last crumb of roll on the windowsill for morning. Corvus tucked his swirly chart under a cushion and did not look at it again.

They slept. The stream, somewhere behind them, kept finding the roots all by itself.
characters: Ash (little elf of still-water eyes), Corvus (sleek night-black crow)
